<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line ltx_leqno">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation</h1>
<span class="ltx_pubnotes ltx_pubnotes_meta"><span class="ltx_pubnotes_content"><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_doi"><span class="ltx_note_name">DOI: </span><a href="https://doi.org/XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX">XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX</a></span><span class="ltx_pubnote ltx_role_ccs"><span class="ltx_note_name">CCS: </span>Computing methodologies Reconstruction</span></span></span>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yi Liu<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>, Xinyi Liu<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>, Yi Wan<sup id="id3" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>, Panwang Xia<sup id="id4" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>, Qiong Wu<sup id="id5" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>, Yongjun Zhang<sup id="id6" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>
<br class="ltx_break"><sup id="id7" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></sup><span id="id8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">School of Remote Sensing and Information Engineering, Wuhan University, Hubei, China
<br class="ltx_break"></span>
</span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates">2025</div>

<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_teaserfigure"><img src="2505.05509v2/fig1.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/166;" width="476" height="166" alt="Figure 1">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1. </span>Visual results achieved by NAFSSR<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, SwinFIRSSR<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and our method on the Flickr1024<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019b</a>)</cite> dataset.<span id="acmlabel1" class="ltx_nodisplay ltx_acm_description">Figure 1</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract.</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Stereo image super-resolution (SSR) aims to enhance high-resolution details by leveraging information from stereo image pairs. However, existing stereo super-resolution (SSR) upsampling methods (e.g., pixel shuffle) often overlook cross-view geometric consistency and are limited to fixed-scale upsampling. The key issue is that previous upsampling methods use convolution to independently process deep features of different views, lacking cross-view and non-local information perception, making it difficult to select beneficial information from multi-view scenes adaptively. In this work, we propose Stereo Implicit Neural Representation (StereoINR), which innovatively models stereo image pairs as continuous implicit representations. This continuous representation breaks through the scale limitations, providing a unified solution for arbitrary-scale stereo super-resolution reconstruction of left-right views. Furthermore, by incorporating spatial warping and cross-attention mechanisms, StereoINR enables effective cross-view information fusion and achieves significant improvements in pixel-level geometric consistency. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets show that StereoINR outperforms out-of-training-distribution scale upsampling and matches state-of-the-art SSR methods within training-distribution scales.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Stereo image super-resolution, cross-view geometry consistency, implicit neural representation.
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1. </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Stereo vision systems are crucial for a range of applications, including 3D reconstruction and autonomous navigation, where high-resolution images are essential for accurate depth estimation and scene understanding. However, existing methods rely on fixed-scale upsampling, which introduces two key issues: 1) These predefined fixed-scale upsampling methods are inflexible. Once the upsampling factor is set, it cannot be adjusted without modifying the model architecture. This limitation severely restricts their practical use in real-world systems that demand adaptable resolution adjustments; 2) Fixed-scale upsampling methods process the local information of each view independently, lacking guidance from global and cross-view information. Therefore, it is urgent to develop novel stereo-upsampling methods that can generate geometrically consistent structures across views based on super-resolution at arbitrary scales.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.05509v2/LAM_for_upsampler-2.png" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:457/277;" width="457" height="277" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2. </span>Local attribution map (LAM) results achieved by different upsampling methods on the Flickr1024 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019b</a>)</cite> dataset. The first row shows the super-resolution results for the left view, while the second and third rows display the LAM results for the left and right views, respectively. Red pixels indicate that the pixel participates in the reconstruction of the pixels in the green rectangle in the result of the left view. DI (Diffusion Index) indicates the range of involved pixels, with a higher DI indicating a wider receptive field.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Arbitrary-scale stereo super-resolution (ASSSR) aims to employ a single model to upscale low-resolution (LR) image pairs to high-resolution (HR) outputs at any appropriate real-valued magnification. Existing stereo super-resolution (SSR) methods  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> typically rely on fixed-scale upsampling techniques (e.g., transposed convolution, pixel shuffling), which limit their flexibility in real scenarios where resolution requirements may vary. Therefore, we introduce Implicit Neural Representation (INR)  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> for arbitrary-scale upsampling, which has been widely used in single image super-resolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lugmayr et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee and Jin, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei and Zhang, 2023</a>)</cite> and video super-resolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. INR treats images as continuous spatial representations and achieves arbitrary-scale super-resolution by learning a coordinate-to-color mapping. Compared to the pixel shuffle method, which integrates local information through convolution, the advantage of the INR method lies in its ability to incorporate attention mechanisms to capture nonlocal and cross-view information. As demonstrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, with INR, our method is able to leverage more pixel information from both views to reconstruct the high-resolution results. Motivated by this, we replace the convolution-based upsampling methods with INR to enhance the cross-view consistency of stereo super-resolution results. This approach not only has the potential to promote geometric consistency in super-resolved images but also overcomes the limitations of fixed-scale methods, offering an effective solution for arbitrary-scale stereo super-resolution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The performance of ASSSR is intricately tied to the representation capacity of the encoded latent features. However, due to the challenge of acquiring paired stereo image data, available stereo training datasets are often limited in scale and quality, leading to suboptimal reconstruction of texture details. In contrast, single-image datasets are more abundant and generally of higher quality. Single-image super-resolution (SISR) methods such as IPT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021b</a>)</cite> and HAT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> leverage large-scale datasets like ImageNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> for pre-training to explore the potential of Transformer. Moreover, ASteISR<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> has demonstrated the feasibility of adapting SISR models to the stereo image domain. Inspired by these methods, we fine-tune the state-of-the-art SISR model on the stereo dataset to fully leverage the prior knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, our goal is to achieve arbitrary-scale stereo image super-resolution and accurately reconstruct geometrically consistent and coherent details across different viewpoints, ensuring structural integrity and realism of high-resolution images in multi-view scenarios. To this end, we proposed StereoINR, which combines two basic components: 1) latent code encoder, and 2) disparity-guided arbitrary-scale up-sampler (DGASU). The latent code encoder captures cross-view correlations, extracts deep features from the left and right images, and provides rich feature representations for subsequent up-sampling reconstruction. The disparity-guided arbitrary-scale upsampling module is based on INR and uses the disparity between the left and right images as guidance. It employs cross-attention to extract beneficial spatial information from different viewpoints, optimizing the upsampling results while maintaining multi-view consistency. This approach helps to maintain the consistency of the cross-view geometry and extract subpixel details from different viewpoints. Besides, since the input coordinates are continuous, we can query image values at any scale, enabling arbitrary scale up-sampling. We highlight our main contributions as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a novel stereo super-resolution framework, named StereoINR. During the upsampling stage, we utilize INR to leverage non-local and cross-view information instead of independently processing features from different viewpoints, enhancing the consistency between the left and right views.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By learning the coordinate-to-color mapping, our method provides a unified solution for stereo image super-resolution across different scales.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Extensive experiments on multiple public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method in achieving high-fidelity stereo image reconstruction. Our framework not only enhances stereo geometry consistency but also effectively handles arbitrary-scale super-resolution, outperforming existing approaches in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2505.05509v2/netarch.png" id="S1.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:457/146;" width="457" height="146" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3. </span>The overall architecture of proposed method. RHAG is the basic block in HAT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> and is frozen during training. The spatial adapter is embedded in the Feed Forward stage of RHAG. The coordinates are randomly sampled from HR image. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2. </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Implicit Neural Representation.</span>
Implicit Neural Representation was initially applied in 3D vision, where NeRF  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mildenhall et al., 2021</a>)</cite> uses spatial coordinates and light direction to implicitly model a 3D scene. Later, LIIF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021a</a>)</cite> introduces implicit neural representations into the field of 2D images, employing MLPs to map image coordinates to RGB values for continuous image representation. Since then, numerous studies  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lugmayr et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2021</a>)</cite> have leveraged improved implicit neural representations instead of traditional up-sampling methods such as pixel shuffling. The merit lies in the fact that INR considers images as continuous representations rather than discrete values, allowing the mapping of continuous 2D coordinates to pixel values and enabling flexible up-sampling at any scale. Therefore, image implicit neural representations have shown remarkable potential in image restoration  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, semantic segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarkar et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, optical flow  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jung et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, disparity estimation  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang and Li, 2024</a>)</cite>, and so on.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2505.05509v2/adapter.svg" id="S2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:457/224;" width="457" height="224"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4. </span>The architecture of the adapter. (a) Stereo adapter, which uses stereo cross attention to achieve left and right view information interaction; (b) Spatial adapter, which modulates input features to adapt to stereo super-resolution; (c) Scale adapter, which uses scale information to modulate input features.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stereo Super Resolution.</span>
Stereo Super Resolution aims to recover high resolution details from a pair of binocular low-resolution images. StereoSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeon et al., 2018</a>)</cite> proposes to leverage stereo images to enhance spatial resolution, which jointly trains a two-stage network of luminance and chrominance to learn the mapping of low and high resolution images. Since the epipolar constraint  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2020</a>)</cite> of the stereo images, we need to pay more attention to the correlation between pixels on the same row on the left and right images. PASSRNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019a</a>)</cite> proposed a parallax attention module to calculate the correlation volume of pixels along the epipolar line. Recently, many methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ying et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> have introduced various cross-attention modules that demonstrate strong performance in stereo super-resolution. However, these approaches typically restrict cross-view information interaction to the deep feature extraction stage, resulting in isolated left and right views during the feature upsampling process. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel upsampling module that leverages disparity constraints inherent in stereo imaging. This module warps deep features using disparity information and incorporates the warped features as auxiliary data, enabling the recovery of high-resolution geometries that are consistent across views.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning in Super Resolution. </span>
Pre-training &amp; fine-tuning can enhance the transferring efficiency and performance in many high-level visual tasks. In low-level vision, IPT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021b</a>)</cite> demonstrates the benefits of multi-task training—covering denoising, deraining, and super-resolution, while EDT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite> pretrains on specific tasks with varied degradation levels, both achieving remarkable results. These approaches underscore the transferability of pretraining across different tasks. For a single task, pre-training leverages the diverse data distributions available in large-scale datasets. HAT<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> demonstrates this by pretraining its model on ImageNet and subsequently fine-tuning on target datasets, thereby enhancing the representation capability of the Transformer architecture. Moreover, ASteISR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> is the first to propose transferring SISR methods to the field of stereo vision. Inspired by these works, we fine-tune the HAT encoder on the stereo datasets using adapter tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3. </span>Methods</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1. </span>Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given any up-sample scale <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, we aim to reconstruct high resolution stereo image pairs <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{L}^{SR},I_{R}^{SR}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times h,r\times w,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{L}^{SR},I_{R}^{SR}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times h,r\times w,3}</annotation></semantics></math> from low resolution inputs <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{L}^{LR},I_{R}^{LR}\in\mathbb{R}^{h,w,3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{L}^{LR},I_{R}^{LR}\in\mathbb{R}^{h,w,3}</annotation></semantics></math>. Given a 2D query coordinates <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in a continuous image domain, the objective of arbitrary-scale stereo super-resolution is to establish a precise mapping between query coordinates and pixel color values:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(1)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{L},s_{R}=I^{SR}_{L}(x),I^{SR}_{R}(x)=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{E}(I_{L}^{LR},I_{R}^{LR}),x;r)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{L},s_{R}=I^{SR}_{L}(x),I^{SR}_{R}(x)=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{E}(I_{L}^{LR},I_{R}^{LR}),x;r),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{L},s_{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{L},s_{R}</annotation></semantics></math> represent the predicted RGB pixel values corresponding to the coordinate <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in the left and right views, respectively. <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the latent code encoder, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the disparity-guided arbitrary-scale up-sampling module. An overview of the proposed framework is presented in Figure <a href="#S1.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2. </span>Adapter tuning latent encoder</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since HAT is designed as a fixed-scale single-image super-resolution method, it lacks awareness of cross-view contextual relationships and multi-scale feature interactions, making its direct transfer to the stereo imaging domain inappropriate. To address this issue, we embed stereo, scale, and spatial adapters into the basic module of HAT, the Residual Hybrid Attention Group (RHAG) module <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>. The architecture of these adapters is shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, the stereo adapter leverage cross-attention to exchange information from left and right views, which is similar to the SCAM in NAFSSR<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The spatial adapter is embedded within the attention module of RHAG, where it compresses and then restores feature dimensions. It projects the original input dimension <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> to a lower-dimensional space <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, allowing control over the number of parameters in the adapter by adjusting the value of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>. Typically, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\ll d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\ll d</annotation></semantics></math>. In the output stage, a second feed-forward sub-layer restores the original input dimension, projecting <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> back to <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> as the final output of the spatial adapter module. As for the scale adapter, we adopt a structure similar to the channel attention block, modulating scale information along the channel dimension, which can be formulated as:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle e</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathrm{MLP}(s)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>MLP</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathrm{MLP}(s),</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\odot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the element-wise multiplication, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{MLP}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>MLP</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{MLP}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the MLP projector, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{LN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>LN</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{LN}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes LayerNorm, <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{in}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{in}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input feature, and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{out}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{out}</annotation></semantics></math> is the feature after modulation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">It is noteworthy that our method differs from ASteISR<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> in that we aim for making the features extracted by the Encoder universally applicable to detail reconstruction at arbitrary scales. To accomplish this, we explicitly inject scale-specific information into the scale adapter, allowing dynamic parameter modulation that adaptively adjusts features for different scaling factors. This design fundamentally enhances the model’s generalization capability for multi-resolution tasks, setting it apart from fixed-scale approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the latent codes for the left and right viewpoints are obtained through the fine-tuned encoder <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>

</div>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3. </span>Disparity guided arbitrary scale upsampler</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After getting the latent codes with the deep feature extractor, we aim at generating a stereo continuous image representation for stereo image pairs. Initially, we estimate the disparity between the left and right view images:</p>

<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{disp}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>disp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{disp}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a state-of-the-art disparity estimator. <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{L\rightarrow R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{L\rightarrow R}</annotation></semantics></math> is employed to align the latent encoding of the right view with the left view, while <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{R\rightarrow L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{R\rightarrow L}</annotation></semantics></math> is used to align the latent encoding of the left view with the right view:</p>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{warp}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>warp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{warp}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the standard image/feature warping operation using the bilinear kernel.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address the challenge of information extraction under complex multiview conditions while mitigating occlusion interference, we employ a cross-attention mechanism for adaptive spatial information aggregation across viewpoints. This architecture uses attention-based feature alignment to dynamically compute inter-view attention scores, enabling: 1) selective emphasis on geometrically consistent and semantically complementary cues from non-occluded regions, and 2) effective suppression of conflicting signals due to texture ambiguities, parallax discontinuities, and partial occlusions. The learned attention weights facilitate optimal information fusion, enhancing feature discriminability while maintaining robustness against cross-view appearance variations. As depicted in Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.2. Adapter tuning latent encoder ‣ 3. Methods ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, the query <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(Q_{L},Q_{R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(Q_{L},Q_{R})</annotation></semantics></math> is derived from the latent codes of the current viewpoint, while the key <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(K_{R\rightarrow L},K_{L\rightarrow R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(K_{R\rightarrow L},K_{L\rightarrow R})</annotation></semantics></math> and the value <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(V_{R\rightarrow L},V_{L\rightarrow R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(V_{R\rightarrow L},V_{L\rightarrow R})</annotation></semantics></math> are constructed through aligned latent codes:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E9"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(9)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Q_{L}=W_{q}^{L}z_{L},K_{R\rightarrow L}=W_{k}^{L}z_{R\rightarrow L},V_{R\rightarrow L}=W_{v}^{L}z_{R\rightarrow L}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Q_{L}=W_{q}^{L}z_{L},K_{R\rightarrow L}=W_{k}^{L}z_{R\rightarrow L},V_{R\rightarrow L}=W_{v}^{L}z_{R\rightarrow L},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E10"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(10)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle Q_{R}=W_{q}^{R}z_{R},K_{L\rightarrow R}=W_{k}^{R}z_{L\rightarrow R},V_{L\rightarrow R}=W_{v}^{R}z_{L\rightarrow R}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>R</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>R</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>R</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Q_{R}=W_{q}^{R}z_{R},K_{L\rightarrow R}=W_{k}^{R}z_{L\rightarrow R},V_{L\rightarrow R}=W_{v}^{R}z_{L\rightarrow R}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Then we calculate the similarity between queries and keys to generate learnable attention weights, which are applied to perform a weighted summation of value vectors, ultimately achieving cross-view feature fusion:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E11"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle F_{L}=\mathrm{softmax}(\frac{Q_{L}K_{R\rightarrow L}}{\sqrt{C}})V_{R\rightarrow L}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>softmax</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><msqrt><mi>C</mi></msqrt></mfrac></mstyle><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle F_{L}=\mathrm{softmax}(\frac{Q_{L}K_{R\rightarrow L}}{\sqrt{C}})V_{R\rightarrow L},</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the feature channel of the query vectors. To further enhance feature selection and aggregation, we implement a variant of the squeeze and excitation mechanism as a form of global self-attention. It computes the refined features <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\widetilde{z}_{L},\widetilde{z}_{R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>R</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\widetilde{z}_{L},\widetilde{z}_{R})</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(F_{L},F_{R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(F_{L},F_{R})</annotation></semantics></math> with reference to <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(z_{L},z_{R})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(z_{L},z_{R})</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E13"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(13)</span></td>

<tbody id="S3.E14"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\widetilde{z}_{R}=z_{R}+\mathrm{Conv}(F_{R})+F_{R}\odot\mathrm{sigmoid}(\mathrm{Conv}(F_{R}))." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>Conv</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>sigmoid</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Conv</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\widetilde{z}_{R}=z_{R}+\mathrm{Conv}(F_{R})+F_{R}\odot\mathrm{sigmoid}(\mathrm{Conv}(F_{R})).</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Then, given a 2d coordinate <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, we formulate the coordinate-to-color mapping as an MLP <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2+C}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2+C}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}</annotation></semantics></math> that predicts the corresponding RGB values conditioned on spatial coordinates, where <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the learnable network parameters.</p>
<table id="S3.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(15)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{L},s_{R}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast},x-x^{\ast})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{L},s_{R}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast},x-x^{\ast}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast})</annotation></semantics></math> are the nearest latent codes from the query coordinate <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\ast}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\ast}</annotation></semantics></math> is the coordinate of the latent codes <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast})</annotation></semantics></math> in the image domain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Vanilla MLPs that employ ReLU activation functions exhibit inherent spectral bias <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rahaman et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee and Jin, 2022</a>)</cite>, tending to capture low-frequency content. To address this problem, we map the input coordinates into a high-dimensional space by sinusoidal positional encoding and concatenate it with the latent codes.</p>
<table id="S3.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E16"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(16)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\gamma(x)=\mathrm{concat}(x,cos(\pi x),sin(\pi x),\dots,cos(n\pi x),sin(n\pi x))." lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\gamma(x)=\mathrm{concat}(x,cos(\pi x),sin(\pi x),\dots,cos(n\pi x),sin(n\pi x)).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Previous INR methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei and Zhang, 2023</a>)</cite> aggregated features by stacking multiple self-attention layers. We improve feature aggregation by alternating between self-attention and cross-attention, facilitating more effective information exchange between the left and right views. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.2. Adapter tuning latent encoder ‣ 3. Methods ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we aggregate multiple views information using alternating self-attention and cross-attention mechanisms. Finally, the MLP is adapted to output the predicted color values, which are then combined with the bicubic-upsampled input image pair through a LR skip connection to obtain the final super-resolution results.</p>
<table id="S3.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(17)</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{L},s_{R}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast},\gamma(x-x^{\ast})))+\mathrm{Bilinear}(I_{L}^{LR}(x),I_{R}^{LR}(x))." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>L</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>Bilinear</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{L},s_{R}=\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(\widetilde{z}_{L}^{\ast},\widetilde{z}_{R}^{\ast},\gamma(x-x^{\ast})))+\mathrm{Bilinear}(I_{L}^{LR}(x),I_{R}^{LR}(x)).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4. </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1. </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Datasets</span>. Our training and validation datasets are provided by iPASSR, sourced from Middlebury <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scharstein et al., 2014</a>)</cite> and Flickr1024 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019a</a>)</cite>. Specifically, we utilize 860 pairs of stereo images for training and 112 pairs for validation. To evaluate the generalization capability of our method, we employ the KITTI 2012 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiger et al., 2012</a>)</cite> and KITTI 2015 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Menze and Geiger, 2015</a>)</cite> test sets for comprehensive assessment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training Details</span>. We use <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>96</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 96</annotation></semantics></math> patches as the inputs of the encoder. Let <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> denote the training batch size, we first sample <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> random scales <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r^{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r^{i}</annotation></semantics></math> following a continuous uniform distribution <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}(1,4)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}(1,4)</annotation></semantics></math>, then we crop <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> patches with sizes <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{64\times r^{i},96\times r^{i}\}^{B}_{i=1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>96</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{64\times r^{i},96\times r^{i}\}^{B}_{i=1}</annotation></semantics></math> from training image pairs. <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>96</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 96</annotation></semantics></math> inputs are their down-sampled counterpart. For the ground truths, we converted these images to pixel samples (coordinate-RGB pairs) and we sample <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>96</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 96</annotation></semantics></math> pixel samples for each of them so that the shapes of ground-truths are the same in a batch, as is done in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021a</a>)</cite>. We use L1 loss and the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>. All models are trained for 200000 iterations with batch size <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> per GPU, and the learning rate decays by the cosine annealing. In addition, we use SPyNet<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ranjan and Black, 2017</a>)</cite> to estimate the disparity between the left and right views for spatial warping. SPyNet is usually used to estimate the optical flow of video sequences. Since the horizontal optical flow in stereo pairs is equivalent to the disparity under rectified settings, we use its horizontal optical flows to perform spatial warping. During training, we fine-tune only the stereo-aware adapter, scale-aware adapter, spatial adapter, and disparity-guided arbitrary scale upsampler, while keeping all other parameters frozen.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2. </span>
Quantitative results achieved by different methods on the KITTI 2012 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiger et al., 2012</a>)</cite>, Middlebury <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scharstein et al., 2014</a>)</cite>, and Flickr1024 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2019a</a>)</cite> datasets.
# Tuned represents the number of trained parameters of the networks.
Here, SCORE<math id="S4.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>, PSNR<math id="S4.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>, and SSIM<math id="S4.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math> values achieved on a pair of stereo images (i.e., (Left+Right)/2) are reported.
<span id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Red</span> and <span id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">blue</span> colors indicate the best and the second-best performance, respectively.
</figcaption>
<div id="S4.T2.6" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:104.5pt;vertical-align:-51.2pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-228.6pt,69.2pt) scale(0.430028029710344,0.430028029710344) ;">
<table id="S4.T2.6.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T2.6.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Method</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.6.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text">Scale</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.6.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" rowspan="2"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text">#Tuned</span></td>
<td id="S4.T2.6.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" colspan="3"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SCORE <math id="S4.T2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></td>

<td id="S4.T2.6.1.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" colspan="3"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">SSIM <math id="S4.T2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math></span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.6.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T2.6.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T2.6.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S4.T2.6.1.2.1.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T2.6.1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">

<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation Metrics</span>. As the most widely used metrics for assessing image quality, PSNR and SSIM are not always consistent with the visual perception of the human eye. LPIPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018a</a>)</cite> is a learned perceptual image patch similarity metric designed to assess image quality in a manner that closely aligns with human visual perception. In order to measure the cross-view consistency of stereo images, NTIRE 2023  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> introduces Score to assess the quality of stereoscopic images by disparity:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle SCORE=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>O</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle SCORE=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle 1-0.5\times(\mathcal{P}(I_{L}^{SR},I_{L}^{HR})+\mathcal{P}(I_{R}^{SR},I_{R}^{HR}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle 1-0.5\times(\mathcal{P}(I_{L}^{SR},I_{L}^{HR})+\mathcal{P}(I_{R}^{SR},I_{R}^{HR}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left">(18)</span></td>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E18.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle-0.1\times\mathcal{L}(D^{SR},D^{HR})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle-0.1\times\mathcal{L}(D^{SR},D^{HR}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Where <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes LPIPS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018a</a>)</cite> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(D^{SR},D^{HR})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(D^{SR},D^{HR})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the MAE between disparity maps <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{SR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{SR}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{HR}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{HR}</annotation></semantics></math>. To evaluate the stereo consistency, we used a pre-trained model such as RAFT-Stereo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Teed and Deng, 2020</a>)</cite> to estimate the disparity from SR and HR pairs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2. </span>Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since INR provides a foundation for arbitrary-scale stereo super-resolution, we divide the quantitative experimental comparisons into two parts:
1) Out-scale: Comparison with other arbitrary-scale super-resolution methods beyond the training scales (×4+);
2) In-scale: Comparison with current fixed-scale super-resolution methods on scales covered by the training data (×2–×4) to validate our method’s performance within trained scales.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quantitive results.</span>
To validate the effectiveness of our method in both out-of-scale and in-scale stereo super-resolution, we conduct two sets of comparisons with state-of-the-art methods.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For out-of-scale upsampling, we compare our method with other INR-based methods, such as LIIF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021a</a>)</cite>, LTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee and Jin, 2022</a>)</cite>, LINF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, OPE-SR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and EQSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, for arbitrary-scale upsampling, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3. Disparity guided arbitrary scale upsampler ‣ 3. Methods ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. For a fair comparison, we retrained the other methods on the stereo image dataset. Since large-scale super-resolution significantly degrades geometric information, comparing disparity results becomes less meaningful. Therefore, we evaluate performance using PSNR and perceptual loss (LPIPS), and our method achieves the best performance for out-of-scale upsampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For in-scale upsampling, we compare our method with fixed-scale super-resolution approaches, including EDSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, RDN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2018b</a>)</cite>, StereoSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jeon et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, iPASSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, SSRDEFNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, NAFSSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and SwinFIRSSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.1. Implementation Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Our method demonstrates competitive performance in terms of PSNR and SSIM while achieving a significant improvement in stereo consistency (SCORE). These results indicate that our approach successfully preserves multi-view geometric consistency during the upsampling process. Furthermore, although trained on the Flickr1024 and Middlebury datasets, our model also performs well on the KITTI dataset, indicating its generalization capability across different datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qualitative results.</span> The in-scale qualitative results are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.1. Implementation Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 3.3. Disparity guided arbitrary scale upsampler ‣ 3. Methods ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, where we compare our method with existing fixed-scale stereo super-resolution approaches at a <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>4 scale. Our method effectively utilizes complementary information from different viewpoints to recover fine details, particularly in complex textures such as walls and grounds. We also annotate each image with its corresponding SCORE and observe that images with higher SCORE exhibit superior restoration of both textures and geometric structures, thereby validating the effectiveness of SCORE as a metric for stereo consistency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we evaluated the disparity results of super-resolution images generated by different methods. Using RAFT-Stereo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Teed and Deng, 2020</a>)</cite>, we estimate the disparity of the SR results, including those produced by SwinFIRSSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and NAFSSR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 4.1. Implementation Details ‣ 4. Experiments ‣ StereoINR: Cross-View Geometry Consistent Stereo Super Resolution with Implicit Neural Representation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, our method produces more consistent cross-view geometry and generates more accurate disparity maps compared to other methods.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.4.1.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
